description: A team made up of 3 computer engineers and 2 robotics engineers, eager to bring ideas to life and be part of something big.
summary: FloodyLens is a satellite-based flood detection prototype that turns Earth observation data into accessible information for emergency response. We developed a Python processing workflow and an interactive map to compare satellite images from different dates, highlight potential newly flooded areas, and help users explore changes on the ground. Our prototype investigates the October 2024 Valencia floods using Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar imagery, with additional exploration of NASA–ISRO NISAR data. Radar observations enable monitoring through clouds and at night, when optical imagery may be unavailable. FloodyLens addresses the challenge by connecting satellite data analysis with a practical visual tool for understanding flood impacts. It aims to help emergency services and local authorities assess affected areas and prioritize further investigation. Floods can evolve rapidly, while reliable information is often fragmented or difficult to interpret. By making satellite observations easier to understand, FloodyLens supports more informed decisions and better coordination. The current results are exploratory and require validation before operational use. Currently, FloodyLens is a functional exploratory prototype visualizing potentially flooded areas on an interactive map using satellite imagery (Valencia case study). In the future, we aim to validate and automate the system into a reliable, real-time tool for emergency services and citizens.
details:
FloodyLens is a satellite-based flood detection prototype designed to support emergency response and local authorities. It compares images acquired on different dates to identify potential newly flooded areas and display them in an interactive map. Developed using Python and radar imagery, the prototype explores the October 2024 Valencia floods using Sentinel-1 data, alongside additional experiments with NASA–ISRO NISAR imagery. Its goal is to turn satellite observations into accessible information that helps emergency teams assess affected areas and coordinate their response. Results are exploratory and require validation.
